Study Questions 2 --- BIOL 126

=======================================================================

PLEASE READ THESE INSTRUCTIONS CAREFULLY BEFORE BEGINNING THE STUDY QUESTIONS =======================================================================

These study questions are designed to help you learn and practice the material from Unit 2 (Phylogenetic Diversity, Extinction Rates, Biodiversity–Ecosystem Function, and Values of Biodiversity). The problems here span the full range of difficulty, from straightforward introductory questions up through harder problems that are directly comparable to what you will find in the graded homework and quiz.

We strongly suggest that you watch all of the lecture videos and complete the associated readings if you run into a problem that is unfamiliar. Unit 2 content begins at lecture 2.4 (Phylogenetic Diversity).

Please be sure to work through these study questions, and especially the explanations (using the ? icon — see below), before asking for help with the homework or quiz.

A few notes on the study questions:

  • problems are either multiple-answer (select all that apply) or have a text entry box for numeric answers
    • many (but not all) of the multiple-answer questions could have more than one correct answer; always read the question carefully and select all answers that apply.
    • if you see a text entry box, that means you should enter a number. Do not enter any other text besides the numeric value, or it will not be graded as correct.
  • each problem has icons below the answer options or answer entry box:
    • at the bottom left of each question is a checkmark ✔️ icon: use this to check your answer once you've entered it
    • the checkmark icon converts to a ↰ icon once you have submitted your answer; you can hit ↰ to clear your response and try again (whether you got it right or wrong)
    • at the bottom right, there is a question mark ? icon: use this to show an explanation of how to work through the problem. This is the most important feature of the study questions! We suggest trying the problem first without looking at the explanation, and consulting it only after you've made an attempt. Even if you get a problem right on the first try, it's worth reading the explanation carefully.
    • also at the bottom right is a refresh ↺ icon: clicking this generates a new variant of the problem. The question framing stays the same but the numbers or answer choices change. You can revisit study questions as many times as you like — the variety in the pool means each attempt may look a little different. There are 3 different variants of each problem.
    • even if you get a problem right on the first try, we recommend trying at least one or two other variants to build confidence.

In the phylogenetic tree below, which species is/are most closely related to species d? Select all that apply.

(Hint: the most closely related species are the ones that share the most recent common ancestor with species d.)

The most closely related species to species d is/are species c.

To find the answer, follow the branch leading to species d back (to the left) until it meets the first vertical line — that node is the most recent common ancestor of species d and its closest relatives. All of the species descending from that node (other than species d itself) share that ancestor, and are therefore equally closely related to species d.

In the diagram below, species d is shown in orange. The blue lines trace the lineage of its closest relative(s): species c.

A conservation organization can fund reserves for exactly three of the species shown in the phylogenetic tree below. Which set of three species would protect the greatest amount of evolutionary history (phylogenetic diversity)?

The set with the highest phylogenetic diversity is species b, d, e.

To find this, start at the first (oldest) divergence event — the leftmost vertical line in the tree. To maximize evolutionary history, you need at least one species from each of the two main groups that split there. Then look at the older of those two lineages: follow it to the right and find where it diverges next. Again, pick one species from each daughter lineage. Occasionally a lineage has only one species — in that case it represents maximum diversity for that branch.

In the diagram below, the three major evolutionary lineages are highlighted in different colors. A set maximizing phylogenetic diversity contains one species from each color group. You can see that species b, d, e each belong to a different color group.

The set(s) with the highest phylogenetic diversity is/are: species a, b, e; species a, b, c; species a, b, h; species a, b, f.

Tropical birds are among the most species-rich and most threatened groups of vertebrates on Earth. Suppose that background extinction rates for tropical forest birds are estimated to be approximately 5 extinction(s) per 10,000 species per year. A survey of a large tropical forest region identifies approximately 5,000 bird species.

How many bird species would be expected to go extinct in that region in a single year under background extinction rates? Round to the nearest whole number.

We would expect 2 extinction(s) per year given these parameters.

The calculation is straightforward:

\[\frac{5 \text{ extinctions}}{10{,}000 \text{ species per year}} \times 5,000\text{ species}\]

The units of "species" cancel from numerator and denominator, leaving us with extinctions per year:

\[= \frac{5 \times 5,000}{10{,}000} = \frac{25000}{10{,}000} = 2.5\]

Rounded to the nearest whole number: 2 extinction(s).

Note: in the homework and quiz, you will encounter the same type of calculation but with the rate expressed as extinctions per million species per year (E/MSY). The process is identical — just substitute 1,000,000 in the denominator instead of 10,000.

Biologists studying extinction trends in tropical forest birds compiled records from museum collections, field surveys, and published reports. Over the last 50 years, 60 bird species in the region are documented to have gone extinct. Based on fossil evidence and long-term background rates, scientists estimate that only 4 species would have been expected to go extinct over that same 50-year period under background conditions.

By what factor is the current (observed) extinction rate higher than the background (historical) rate? Round your answer to one decimal place.

The current extinction rate is 15 times higher than the background rate.

We calculate this as:

\[\frac{\text{observed extinctions}}{\text{expected extinctions}} = \frac{60}{4} = 15\]

Rounded to one decimal place: 15.

Note: in the homework and quiz, the observed and expected counts are derived from background rates given in E/MSY (extinctions per million species per year). The ratio calculation here is identical — the only difference is how the expected count is computed first.

Biologists studying extinction trends in tropical forest birds compiled records from museum collections, field surveys, and published reports. Over the last 50 years, 35 bird species in the region are documented to have gone extinct. Based on fossil evidence and long-term background rates, scientists estimate that only 3 species would have been expected to go extinct over that same 50-year period under background conditions.

By what factor is the current (observed) extinction rate higher than the background (historical) rate? Round your answer to one decimal place.

The current extinction rate is 11.7 times higher than the background rate.

We calculate this as:

\[\frac{\text{observed extinctions}}{\text{expected extinctions}} = \frac{35}{3} = 11.6666667\]

Rounded to one decimal place: 11.7.

Note: in the homework and quiz, the observed and expected counts are derived from background rates given in E/MSY (extinctions per million species per year). The ratio calculation here is identical — the only difference is how the expected count is computed first.

Biologists studying extinction trends in tropical forest birds compiled records from museum collections, field surveys, and published reports. Over the last 50 years, 45 bird species in the region are documented to have gone extinct. Based on fossil evidence and long-term background rates, scientists estimate that only 3 species would have been expected to go extinct over that same 50-year period under background conditions.

By what factor is the current (observed) extinction rate higher than the background (historical) rate? Round your answer to one decimal place.

The current extinction rate is 15 times higher than the background rate.

We calculate this as:

\[\frac{\text{observed extinctions}}{\text{expected extinctions}} = \frac{45}{3} = 15\]

Rounded to one decimal place: 15.

Note: in the homework and quiz, the observed and expected counts are derived from background rates given in E/MSY (extinctions per million species per year). The ratio calculation here is identical — the only difference is how the expected count is computed first.

Based on fossil evidence and long-term background rates, scientists estimate that only 3 species would have been expected to go extinct over that same 50-year period under background conditions.

Estimates from tropical bird surveys suggest that current bird extinction rates are approximately 20 times higher than the background extinction rate. Assume the background extinction rate is 1 species extinction per 10,000 species per year. There are approximately 8,000 tropical bird species.

How many tropical bird species would be expected to go extinct in a single year at the current (elevated) rate? Round to the nearest whole number.

We would expect approximately 16 extinction(s) per year under current rates.

Since the background rate is 1 per 10,000 species per year, and current rates are 20 times higher, the current rate is:

\[\frac{20 \text{ extinctions}}{10{,}000 \text{ species per year}}\]

Multiplying by the total number of species (and by 1 year) gives:

\[\frac{20}{10{,}000} \times 8,000\text{ species} = \frac{160000}{10{,}000} = 16\]

Rounded: 16 extinction(s).

Note: in the homework and quiz, the background rate is given in E/MSY (extinctions per million species per year) and species counts are in the millions. The logic is the same — substitute 1,000,000 for 10,000 and millions of species for thousands.

Ecologists set up experimental grassland plots with varying levels of plant species richness and measured net primary productivity (the amount of biomass produced per year) in each plot. The data from this fictional experiment are shown below.

Does this dataset show a biodiversity–ecosystem function (BEF) relationship?

There is no relationship between plant species richness and grassland productivity in this dataset; the slope of the line is not distinguishable from zero. Primary productivity is roughly the same regardless of how many plant species are present. The dotted line in the graph below shows the fitted relationship: flat (slope ≈ 0) when there is no BEF, or upward when there is a positive BEF.

Which of the following are examples of instrumental values of biodiversity? (Select all that apply.)

Instrumental value means that biodiversity is valuable because of the benefits it provides to humans — either directly (food, medicine, materials, recreation), indirectly (ecosystem services such as water purification, pollination, climate regulation, and coastal protection), or as potential future value (option value, a subtype of instrumental value).

The incorrect answers describe: - Intrinsic value: species have worth independent of any human benefit or awareness. - Relational value: value arises from personal or cultural relationships with nature. - Moral/ethical/religious value: conservation is motivated by duty, obligation, or spiritual teaching rather than benefit.

Which of the following are examples of intrinsic values of biodiversity? (Select all that apply.)

Intrinsic value means that biodiversity has worth in and of itself — independent of any benefit to humans, any personal relationship with nature, and any sense of duty or obligation. The defining test: would the species or ecosystem have value even if no human existed?

The incorrect answers describe: - Instrumental value: biodiversity is valuable for the benefits it provides to humans. - Relational value: value arises from ongoing personal or cultural relationships with nature. - Moral/ethical/religious value: conservation is motivated by duty, obligation, or sacred teaching — which invokes human responsibility rather than inherent worth.

Which of the following are examples of relational values of biodiversity? (Select all that apply.)

Relational value arises from the ongoing relationships between people and the natural world — personal memories, cultural identity, sense of place, and practices (foraging, fishing, ceremony, recreation) that connect individuals or communities to specific species or landscapes. The value is constituted by the relationship itself, not by what the biodiversity produces economically and not by an abstract duty or obligation.

Key distinctions: - Moral/ethical/religious distractors invoke a duty or obligation — the conservation imperative comes from what is right to do, not from a lived relationship. - Intrinsic value distractors hold that species have worth regardless of any human experience — the value is entirely independent of relationship. - Instrumental value distractors point to economic or material benefit — the value is about what biodiversity produces for humans.

Which of the following are examples of option values of biodiversity? (Select all that apply.)

Option value is a subtype of instrumental value based on potential future human benefit---benefits that are not yet known or realized. The key criterion: we don't know exactly what the benefit will be in the future, but we want to preserve the possibility. This is distinct from:

  • Current instrumental value (known, realized benefit to people — e.g., pollination happening right now)
  • Intrinsic value (value independent of human benefit, known or unknown)
  • Relational value (value arising from personal/cultural relationships)
  • Moral/ethical value (conservation as duty or obligation)

Which of the following are examples of moral, ethical, or religious reasons for conserving biodiversity? (Select all that apply.)

Moral, ethical, and religious reasons for conservation are grounded in duty, obligation, or sacred teaching — the conservation imperative comes from what is right to do (or what is divinely commanded), independent of personal relationship and independent of economic benefit.

Key distinctions that students commonly miss: - Relational value distractors involve a personal or cultural bond with a specific place or species — the motivation is the relationship itself, not an abstract obligation. - Intrinsic value distractors hold that species have worth regardless of any human experience — similar to moral/ethical in being independent of benefit, but distinct in that it does not invoke duty or obligation.

Note: Some examples (such as traditional teachings about restrained harvesting) can involve both relational and moral/religious elements. When a teaching is framed as a sacred obligation rather than a personal bond, it falls primarily in the moral/religious category.

Which of the following are examples of moral, ethical, or religious reasons for conserving biodiversity? (Select all that apply.)

Moral, ethical, and religious reasons for conservation are grounded in duty, obligation, or sacred teaching — the conservation imperative comes from what is right to do (or what is divinely commanded), independent of personal relationship and independent of economic benefit.

Key distinctions that students commonly miss: - Relational value distractors involve a personal or cultural bond with a specific place or species — the motivation is the relationship itself, not an abstract obligation. - Intrinsic value distractors hold that species have worth regardless of any human experience — similar to moral/ethical in being independent of benefit, but distinct in that it does not invoke duty or obligation.

Note: Some examples (such as traditional teachings about restrained harvesting) can involve both relational and moral/religious elements. When a teaching is framed as a sacred obligation rather than a personal bond, it falls primarily in the moral/religious category.
